Title: The big winners and losers in U.S. website traffic over the past year

URL Source: https://searchengineland.com/winners-losers-us-website-traffic-past-year-486843

Published Time: 2026-09-04T15:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
[Google Analytics 4](https://searchengineland.com/guide/how-to-use-google-analytics-4)(GA4) became mandatory on July 1, 2023, when standard Universal Analytics properties stopped processing new data. Less than a year later, on May 14, 2024, Google began rolling out AI Overviews to U.S. users.

The timing matters: The industry lost a clean, comparable measurement baseline just as search traffic patterns started to shift. So, over the past 12 months, who gained website traffic in the U.S., and who lost it?

The Semrush Traffic Analytics tool tracks the most visited websites in the U.S. and updates the list monthly, making it one of the few sources that can answer that question with real numbers rather than vibes.

I pulled the data as of July 2026 and compared it against the same period a year earlier. What I found confirms some of what you’d expect and contradicts the rest.

## The giants didn’t move. Their traffic did.

The top of the list looks almost identical to how it looked a year ago.

*   Google still ranks first in the U.S., with 25.3 billion monthly visits. 
*   YouTube is still second, at 10.3 billion. 
*   Reddit is still third, at 2.61 billion. 

If you only glanced at these rankings, you’d conclude that nothing had changed. You’d be wrong. Google’s traffic is up 10.72% year over year. YouTube is up a startling 36.6% compared to a year ago.

Between them, Google and YouTube now account for a huge share of all attention at the top of the web, and the top three sites alone generate 54.3% of the top 10’s traffic. Concentration at the very top hasn’t loosened. If anything, it’s tightened.

That stability is itself the headline. Total visits across the top 150 U.S. sites only rose 6.1% year over year, and the top 10 still account for 68.6% of all of it, almost unchanged from 68.8% a year ago.

The web isn’t getting less concentrated as AI changes search. It’s getting more so, just with a couple of new names inside the circle.

[Be the brand AI recommends. See where your brand appears in AI search, where competitors are winning, and what it takes to become the answer AI recommends. See your AI visibility](https://www.semrush.com/ai-seo/overview?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0101ai&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## The clearest winner: ChatGPT

If you want one number that captures how much the search landscape has shifted, it’s this one: ChatGPT.com is up 48.38% year over year, now ranking ninth among all U.S. websites with 1.09 billion monthly visits, ahead of DuckDuckGo and Bing.

A year ago, that sentence would’ve read differently. Today, an AI chatbot outranks a couple of search engines that have been around since 2008 and 2009.

TikTok, by comparison, ranks 14th with 573.6 million visits and a much more modest 1.63% year-over-year gain. So, it’s not that “new platforms” are winning across the board — it’s specifically that generative AI usage has moved from novelty to habit fast enough to show up as one of the single-biggest traffic gains anywhere in the top 20.

A few other winners are worth flagging because they aren’t AI chatbots:

*   **LinkedIn** climbed from 21st to 19th place, with visits up 15.48% year over year to 473.7 million — enough to push it into the top 20 for the first time in this data set.
*   **USPS.com** is up 12.04% year over year, a reminder that utility and habit still drive traffic even in an AI-saturated news cycle.
*   **Twitch** climbed five spots to 25th after a 25.6% jump in visits.
*   **Comix.to**, further down the list, posted the single-largest percentage gain of any site I looked at, jumping 14 places (70th to 56th) on a 37.3% increase in visits.

## The losers are more interesting than the winners

Here’s what surprised me: The steepest year-over-year decline in the entire top 20 doesn’t belong to a struggling news site or a fading social network. It belongs to Bing, which is down 50.43% year over year.

Microsoft has spent three years and enormous sums bolting Copilot onto Bing to convert AI hype into search share, and the traffic data suggests that bet still hasn’t paid off the way Redmond hoped.

Bing’s standalone search share has been essentially flat against Google for years, and this year’s numbers look like a continuation of that pattern rather than a break from it.

Temu is the other big decliner, down 28.55% year over year. That one has a clear, well-documented cause.

The closure of the “de minimis” tariff exemption on low-value Chinese imports in mid-2025 gutted the pricing advantage that built Temu’s U.S. business in the first place, and reporting at the time showed Temu’s U.S. ad spend and app rankings collapsing in tandem with the policy change.

This wasn’t an SEO story or an AI story. It was a trade policy story that happened to show up in traffic data.

The rest of the losers list is a mix of the predictable and the genuinely surprising:

*   Amazon, down 15.31% year over year — a notable decline for a site whose traffic is usually treated as a bellwether for ecommerce health.
*   Yahoo, down 13.82%.
*   DuckDuckGo, down 15.83%, which is worth sitting with given that it’s a search engine, not a social network or a retailer.
*   ESPN fell from 19th to 24th (visits down 16.0% to 366.0 million).
*   NBCNews.com dropped 35 spots to 145th, with visits down 20.2%.

None of these losses are identical in cause. But taken together, they say something the top-line “Google and YouTube are still winning” narrative doesn’t: Traffic is being redistributed, unevenly and for different reasons, well below the top three positions everyone already watches.

## Here’s the part that should worry SEOs

Jes Scholz wrote a piece back in February called “[Why GA4 alone can’t measure the real impact of AI SEO](https://searchengineland.com/why-ga4-alone-cant-measure-the-real-impact-of-ai-seo-468387),” arguing that relying on GA4 by itself leaves AI SEO measurement lost in what she called the Bermuda Triangle of analytics.

I didn’t fully appreciate how right she was until I looked at a GA4 account that I hadn’t checked out in a year.

For context, I provide pro bono consulting to a niche publishing website. I recently pulled their GA4 traffic acquisition report for Jan. 1 through Aug. 26, 2026, and compared it to the same period in 2025.

On the surface, it looks like great news: sessions up over 105%, engaged sessions up almost 111%, key events up about 80.5%. If you stopped there, you’d tell this publisher they’re winning.

Keep reading the same report, though, and direct traffic is up more than 157% and now accounts for over 78% of their total traffic, up from about 62.5% a year earlier. That means GA4 can’t identify where almost four out of every five visitors came from — and that share is growing every month.

“Direct” isn’t a traffic source. It’s the label GA4 slaps on everything it can’t attribute, and an increasing amount of that unattributed traffic is almost certainly arriving via links generated inside AI chat interfaces, which routinely get stripped of the referrer data that GA4 depends on.

So, is this niche publisher winning? It depends on whether you’re looking backward or forward.

The historical metrics look fantastic. However, the attribution underneath them is getting worse every month, which means the next set of decisions this publisher makes about content and channel investment will be based on data that’s actively losing its ability to explain itself.

## Two rules of Italian driving

There’s a scene in the 1976 movie “The Gumball Rally” where the Italian racer Franco, played by Raul Julia, climbs into his Ferrari Daytona Spyder before a cross-country race, rips the rearview mirror clean off the windshield, and tosses it over his shoulder.

“And now, my friend, the primo rule of Italian driving,” he says. “What’s-a behind me is not important.”

That’s what I’d recommend doing with most of GA4’s 19 default channels at this point — including the AI Assistant channel, which tracks visits arriving from ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Copilot, or Grok. (It excludes Google’s own AI Overviews and AI Mode entirely.)

It’s not a huge loss. According to GA4, only 0.47% of traffic to this same niche publisher’s site has come through the native AI Assistant channel since GA4 added it on May 13, 2026. Whatever AI-driven traffic they’re getting isn’t showing up where it’s supposed to.

This prompted me to create the second rule of Italian driving: Pay more attention to the audience intelligence and market research tools that can see the treacherous road ahead instead of the one behind you.

That list, for SEOs trying to navigate this difficult challenge, includes:

*   **Semrush’s website traffic tracker**, which estimates monthly traffic for any domain or URL and shows where competitor traffic originates, which pages capture it, and which keywords and channels drive growth.
*   **SparkToro’s audience research software**, which surfaces what a target audience reads, watches, listens to, and follows — particularly useful for mapping channel affinities, subreddits, and podcasts that GA4 will never show you.
*   **GWI (Global Web Index)**, which runs pre-profiled consumer panels across more than 50 markets and excels at granular psychographic and behavioral segmentation.
*   **YouGov Profiles**, for continuous survey data on brand perception, shopping habits, and demographics.

SEOs should also just start surveying their own customers directly — combining traditional survey tools that capture direct feedback with analytics tools that decode implicit intent gives you both the exact phrases customers use and the content gaps they reveal.

On the survey side, they should consider using:

*   **SurveyMonkey** for deep segment research, with AI-driven synthesis that groups open-ended responses into themes you can turn directly into content categories.
*   **Typeform** for response rates, thanks to a conversational interface that works well embedded in high-traffic landing pages or posts.
*   **Google Forms** for quick, zero-budget pulse checks that flow straight into a spreadsheet.
*   **Qualtrics** for enterprise-grade logic flows and demographic segmentation.

[If AI can’t find you, customers won’t either. Track your visibility across AI search, uncover missed opportunities, and grow your presence where customers are asking questions. See your AI visibility](https://www.semrush.com/ai-seo/overview?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0102ai&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## Measure what GA4 can’t see

It might seem strange to end an article about website traffic winners and losers with a list of survey tools. But that’s the point.

Google and YouTube are still winning, ChatGPT is gaining ground, Bing and DuckDuckGo are losing for different reasons, and underneath all of it, the tool most SEOs still lean on hardest — GA4 — is becoming less able to tell you which channel any individual visitor belongs to.

So, to be one of next year’s winners instead of next year’s cautionary tale, adopt both rules of Italian driving: Pay less attention to what GA4’s default channels tell you about where your traffic came from, and pay a lot more attention to the audience intelligence and market research tools built to see what GA4 can’t.

## Streaming Is Raising Prices Faster Than Cable Ever Did

Congrats, you cut the cord. Now you have six more cords. Streaming prices are rising three times as fast as inflation, making escaping cable company greed now seem quaint.

![Image 1: Streaming apps.](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/17rep_page4_w-1.jpg?w=2000&h=1126&crop=1)

Illustrated by Brian Taylor 

Yup, you’re getting screwed.

The cost to simply watch new TV shows is up — _way up_ — with streaming services delivering one wearisome price shock after another that rival the worst of the cable and satellite price hikes of yesteryear. Since 2022, streaming prices have risen more than three times as much as inflation (which is _also_ too high).

Behold some not-so-fun facts:

· The price of [Apple TV](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/apple-tv-2/) has tripled. The streamer launched at just $4.99 in 2019. It’s jumped 200 percent despite having the thinnest library — in terms of quantity, at least — of the major streamers.

· [Disney+](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/disney/) is right behind Apple TV. The service launched at $6.99 with no ads in 2019 and has since jumped to $11.99 _with_ ads — or pay a whopping 172 percent more than its launch price.

· [Paramount+](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/paramount-2/)’s cheapest tier is up 80 percent in five years. Netflix Premium is up 125 percent since 2013.

· If you want all eight major streamers without ads or bundle commitments, it’ll cost you about $151 a month. Four years ago, the comparable lineup cost about $90.

So you thought you cut the cord, but now you probably have four, five or six cords — and each is auto-drafting from your bank account so you can keep watching _Love Island_ and _Tulsa King_.

The outlier here is HBO Max, having only climbed 23 percent over six years. HBO has been priced as a premium product for decades, however, and launched its streaming service in 2020 at a higher price point than the other services.

And these numbers hide some recent drama. Apple TV went up 50 percent just in the past year. Peacock’s tiers likewise leapt about 50 percent. (It’s a bit wild that HBO Premium is only $3 more than Peacock Premium Plus, especially when the former gives you dragons and Hogwarts and the latter offers _The Miniature Wife_ and _Married at First Sight._)

Over the course of the past 12 months, streaming rates have collectively risen 11.8 percent. The biggest year of increase was 2023, when the streamers shot up an average of 17.7 percent. A _Hollywood Reporter_ analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows cable and satellite prices, by comparison, rose an annual average of 3.9 percent — excluding a deregulation surge of the late 1980s, when the index peaked at 14 percent. But that was a seismic shift provoked by a federal intervention rather than, say, because _Widow’s Bay_ is a good show, or “we’re pretty sure we can get away with this.”

It’s worth pointing out that streaming hikes have wildly outpaced inflation — even with inflation wildly outpacing what should be inflation. Consumer prices have climbed an average of 3.84 percent annually since 2019, double the Federal Reserve’s 2 percent target. That number might still seem small, but it’s added up to a 33 percent increase in the cost of consumer living, which is why everything besides a Costco hot dog has gotten noticeably more expensive. This is also why streaming price hikes are such a gut punch — annual bumps of 10 or 15 percent compound fast.

At this point, you might be wondering: Does this mean cable TV is now a better deal by comparison?

Not at all, not unless you’re a massive sports fan or are really into the Hallmark Channel (hey, _My Christmas Cowboy_ debuts in December). Fully loaded bundles from the likes of Spectrum and DirecTV cost north of $170.

So what’s the solution? Just quietly suffer? Yes — in one way or another. You could do what your uncle commenting on this story on Facebook will suggest (perhaps in all caps): Buy an over-the-air antenna for $25 and tune into whatever the broadcast gods are willing to give you. But that way lies entertainment despair. Our TV past wasn’t actually better — you were just younger, so everything _seemed_ better.

The best hack comes courtesy of Gen Z, who have reportedly embraced streaming cycling. You subscribe to just one streamer for a month or two, catch up on whatever you want, unsubscribe, then subscribe to another. It’s literally “this one simple trick that streamers hate.” Granted, you’ll fall behind on many shows, and won’t be able to participate in watercooler conversations — but since when have you ever seen anybody standing around a watercooler besides in those HR employee compliance videos?

Title: Copywriting Friday: The best ads don’t create desire, they borrow it

URL Source: https://conversion-rate-experts.com/ads-dont-create-desire-they-borrow-it-copywriting-friday/

Published Time: 2026-09-04

Markdown Content:
[Copywriting Friday](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/articles/#copywriting-friday) highlights the tools and techniques of persuasive content. Some of the examples may seem dated, but the principles are timeless (and critical for conversion rate optimization). Enjoy.

If you’ve studied sales for any length of time, you’ve probably heard the advice to “lead with the benefit.” **But the best direct-response copywriters push it one step further.** The benefit you lead with isn’t something you invent, it’s something you borrow, from a desire your reader already carries.

![Image 1: The best copywriters don’t invent desire, they aim it. See how five ads across three centuries, and Eugene Schwartz’s Life-Force 8, borrow desires readers already have.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/ads-dont-create-desire-they-borrow-it-copywriting-friday-hero.jpg)

It’s decent advice ([depending on context](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/features/)), but while this idea might sound limiting, it’s actually the opposite. The hardest part of persuasion is conjuring desire out of nowhere. It’s much easier to tap into the wanting that is already there, _in everyone_, waiting.

If we can do that, our only job is to aim.

In this Copywriting Friday, we’ll see how copywriters have done this across five different ads from three different centuries. We’ll cover how they:

*   Choose their emotional lever.
*   Aim at a desire that already exists instead of inventing one.
*   Stage the benefit so the reader feels it as they read it.

To see what that looks like, we’ll walk through a hundred years of advertising: a heartbroken bridesmaid, a skinny man getting sand kicked in his face, a classic pianist silencing a room, a soap brand that told women they were beautiful, and a search box that fell in love. Five ads across three centuries, aimed at both sexes, pulling opposite emotions.

Eugene Schwartz put it as plainly as it can be put. In _Breakthrough Advertising_, he wrote:

> “Copy cannot create desire for a product. It can only take the hopes, dreams, fears and desires that already exist in the hearts of millions of people, and focus those already existing desires onto a particular product.”

**The force that makes an ad work, he argued, comes from the market, not from your keyboard.**

So where is that force reliably found? In the sales psychology book _Cashvertising_, author Drew Eric Whitman set out what he called the **Life-Force 8**, the eight wants “biologically programmed” into every one of us.

We can’t confirm the biological basis for his claims, but we fully endorse the Life-Force 8 for copywriters who are looking to _improve their aim_. Here they are:

1.   Survival, enjoyment of life, life extension.
2.   Enjoyment of food and beverages.
3.   Freedom from fear, pain, and danger.
4.   Sexual companionship.
5.   Comfortable living conditions.
6.   To be superior, winning, keeping up with the Joneses.
7.   Care and protection of loved ones.
8.   Social approval.

Appeals built on these eight, Whitman argues, outsell other human wants because you’re plugging into a current that’s already live. We think of the Life-Force 8 as a map that helps us “go deeper on the benefits.” Now that you have the list, you can look at almost any famous ad and watch it reach for one of the eight.

So let’s do that here, to show you what we mean.

## Aiming at a desire that’s already burning

In 1923, The Lambert Company ran a Listerine ad about a woman named Edna. And Edna has a problem. _She’s being left behind._

![Image 2: 1923 Listerine magazine advertisement, ’Often a bridesmaid but never a bride,’ showing Edna watching her friends marry while she is left behind.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/ads-dont-create-desire-they-borrow-it-copywriting-friday-1.jpg)

> “Edna’s case was really a pathetic one. Like every woman, her primary ambition was to marry. Most of the girls of her set were married, or about to be. Yet no one possessed more grace or charm or loveliness than she. And as her birthdays crept towards that tragic thirty-mark, marriage seemed farther from her life than ever. She was often a bridesmaid but never a bride.”

Remember that this is an ad for mouthwash. It could focus on the fact that _fresh breath is more pleasant than halitosis_, but the copywriter aims for needs that run far deeper. If we were to measure the ad against the Life-Force 8 (that were written down far later), how would it do? We rate it as hitting 3, 4, and 8.

*   Freedom from fear (the quiet dread of being left behind).
*   Sexual companionship (Edna wants to marry).
*   Social approval (her whole set is pairing off while she watches).

Mouthwash is the mechanism for the change, but belonging is the benefit. The campaign was widely credited with turning a minor antiseptic into a household name, with sales rising dramatically over the years that followed.

Now jump two decades and swap the target from a woman to a man. In the Charles Atlas ads that ran in the back of comic books from the 1940s on, readers met Mac, a self-described “97-pound weakling” who gets sand kicked in his face.

Here’s one of the _(numerous)_ variations that the ad ran in over the years.

![Image 3: A Charles Atlas ’the insult that made a man out of Mac’ comic-strip advertisement, showing the skinny Mac getting sand kicked in his face at the beach, then returning as a bodybuilder.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/ads-dont-create-desire-they-borrow-it-copywriting-friday-2.jpg)

The ad pulls on many of the same levers as “often a bridesmaid.” Mac, our scrawny weakling, is reaching for freedom from the fear of humiliation, sexual companionship, social approval (see last panel), and being superior. That’s 3, 4, 6, and 8.

Here’s the thing. **Nobody had to teach a scrawny boy to want those things.** The ad simply names them and points at the product.

Both of these examples pull on fear and shame, but the aim doesn’t have to be dark. In 1926, John Caples wrote one of the most successful mail-order ads ever made, for the U.S. School of Music. It’s so famous that you almost certainly know it:

![Image 4: John Caples’s 1926 U.S. School of Music advertisement, headlined ’They laughed when I sat down at the piano. But when I started to play!’](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/ads-dont-create-desire-they-borrow-it-copywriting-friday-3.jpg)

> “They laughed when I sat down at the piano. But when I started to play!”

This ad’s story is pure aspiration. A man everyone assumed was a fraud sits down, plays flawlessly, and the room falls silent, then adoring. It aims at the same social approval and superiority as the Atlas ad, minus the bully. The desire is to be admired. The handle is triumph, not dread.

That’s 6 and 8.

Fast-forward almost 80 years. In 2004, Dove and its agency Ogilvy launched the Campaign for Real Beauty. This was built on research suggesting that only a small fraction of women considered themselves beautiful.

While the beauty industry had spent a century selling products through insecurity, **Dove decided to aim at the same desire, social approval and self-worth, from the opposite side**. Essentially, the message is that you can get 3, 4, and 8 without moulding yourself into what society wants. _You are already enough._ It is the Listerine desire, but turned inside out.

![Image 5: A print advertisement from Dove’s 2004 Campaign for Real Beauty, part of a research-driven push that challenged narrow beauty standards.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/ads-dont-create-desire-they-borrow-it-copywriting-friday-4.jpg)

According to Ad Age, the campaign helped grow Dove sales from $2 billion to $4 billion in three years. As a bonus, you may remember this ad as a viral hit in the early years of the campaign.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DCNEIwxkPlc)

Each of these four examples work by aiming at deep desires the audience already had.

_So here’s a question for your own copy._**Which of the eight primal desires does your product or service actually serve?** A backup service isn’t selling storage. It’s selling the protection of loved ones and freedom from fear. A course isn’t selling skills. It’s selling the desire to be superior, to be admired, and perhaps to be more comfortable (better paid) for it.

This is the strategic layer beneath the familiar “benefits, not features” advice. **Find the primal current, and you don’t need to push nearly as hard.**

## Don’t just state a benefit; stage the scene

Aiming at the right desire is only half the job. A desire named is not a desire felt.

A weaker Listerine ad might have said: “Bad breath can hurt your social life. Use Listerine.” True, but forgettable.

Instead, the image and copy built a scene the reader had to stand in. The friends are marrying off one by one. The birthdays “creeping towards that tragic thirty-mark.” Readers of that ad didn’t note a benefit. They watched one slip away from one specific woman, and put themselves in her shoes.

This sense of _being there_ is a close relative of [future pacing](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/glimp-future-pacing-win-report/), the practice of helping users imagine that they already have their desired result. The Atlas ad does it with the final “Hero of the beach” panel. Caples does it with the pianist’s hands hovering over the keys.

The purest modern example of staging the scene is a 2010 Super Bowl ad from Google called “Parisian Love.” There is no voiceover, product shot, or anything that could be reasonably called a sales pitch. The whole ad is a search box, and someone typing into it.

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnsSUqgkDwU)

Here are the searches:

*   _study abroad_
*   _paris france_
*   _cafes near the louvre_
*   _impress a french girl_
*   _long distance relationship advice_
*   _churches in paris_
*   _how to assemble a crib_

Nobody tells us that a romance began, that he stayed, that they married, or that a baby is coming. We assemble all of it ourselves, out of search queries, in sixty seconds.

The benefit of Google Search is never stated once. It is staged so completely that stating it would break the spell.

Before we close this section, here’s a simple question to help avoid abstraction and stage better scenes.

_Could I point a camera at this?_

The phrase “bad breath can hurt your social life” can be written down, but it can’t be filmed. It’s abstract. This is why the image of Edna that the copywriters have conjured works so hard. The reader isn’t just _watching_ Edna. For one moment, _the reader is Edna_.

## Name the thing standing in your customers’ way

Nobody lies awake wanting _mouthwash_ or a _correspondence course_. So the copy builds a bridge, and it usually does it by naming an enemy.

Listerine popularized a clinical-sounding word most readers had never heard, _halitosis_, and **made it the single thing standing between Edna and everything she wanted**. A few years later Lifebuoy pulled the same move with two initials, _B.O._, running hundreds of tiny comic-strip dramas in which body odor was the hidden reason a romance stalled or a job slipped away. In each case, **an ordinary product was recast as the removal of one specific obstacle between the customer and a Life-Force 8 payoff**.

_What is the “halitosis” in your market?_ The unnamed thing standing between your customer and what they most want. Name it, honestly, and your product becomes the key that removes it.

## The wanting was always there

Of course, Edna wasn’t real. Mac wasn’t real. But the desires those ads borrowed, to belong, to be admired, to keep the people we love safe, have been real in humans for thousands of years, and they aren’t going anywhere.

That’s the whole strategy. **You don’t create the wanting. You find it, you aim at it honestly, and you stage its payoff so vividly your reader feels it before they’ve decided to buy.**

Do that, and your product stops being a thing on a shelf. It becomes the one item standing between your customer and a desire that’s older than advertising itself.

See you next time on Copywriting Friday.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!o073!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffdb97fe0-b16f-474c-9766-4b66e29899f5_2154x48.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!o073!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffdb97fe0-b16f-474c-9766-4b66e29899f5_2154x48.png)

Lauren works at Cursor, the AI coding tool SpaceX just bought.

A few weeks ago, she [posted this](https://x.com/poteto/status/2089369732554404153):

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!arQK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa2279c1e-222a-40e0-ab64-cad173f99210_2378x1228.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!arQK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa2279c1e-222a-40e0-ab64-cad173f99210_2378x1228.png)

Free Cursor Ultra (their $200-a-month top plan) to _anyone_ who **cancels a competitor** and sends her a screenshot.

Every tool gives a boring free trial.

Lauren just added a condition → you only get it if you dump a competitor first.

The only way to claim it is a DM (direct message). So she now has a private chat open with every person who switched, and a built-in excuse to message them again when the free month ends.

People did it and posted the proof:

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OtdZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff22abfce-c39a-4592-841a-b5ec5b9483ef_1560x1510.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OtdZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff22abfce-c39a-4592-841a-b5ec5b9483ef_1560x1510.png)

Every post like that is free marketing for Cursor. I love this so much.

A few days later, another Cursor employee, Tibor, [ran the same play](https://x.com/tibor_tee/status/2090935323324805601), this time with time scarcity (only 24 hours). It worked even better.

Have an employee post the offer from their own account, not the founder’s, not the company’s, **as a person doing people a favor** (and maybe getting in trouble for it). If it comes from the founder or the company → it’s just an ad.

Then:

*   🧾 **Get a proof.** Ask for a cancel screenshot, or better: their last invoice (so you know what they were paying).

*   🎁 **Give free months of your most expensive plan.** Don’t give cash.

*   ⏳ **Put a 24-hour deadline on it** (round two had one at Cursor and it worked).

*   🧩 **Get user feedback.** Send the free month over DM and ask “what made you cancel them?” You’ll get golden insights.

Before the free month ends, you can offer to keep them at whatever they were paying the competitor

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GmlZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd57a274a-a86d-4f0e-a953-12abeb7084d3_1456x819.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GmlZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd57a274a-a86d-4f0e-a953-12abeb7084d3_1456x819.webp)

**That’s it!**

You can publish the cancel screenshots later (ask first). Tons of people canceling your competitor is 10x better than a “us vs them” page or a cringe comparison chart.

See you next week ✌️

Tom

P.S. I wrote about [$0 with a Twist](https://www.marketingideas.com/p/the-0-with-a-twist-strategy) last year (free stuff + one weird condition to get it). This is the same trick, but the condition is “dump my competitor”. Lol.

It will then attach this promotion to your eligible ads, displaying the 20% discount directly in the search results when users look for your products."

To be eligible for this:

*   Active Search or Performance Max campaigns with attached Location Assets (including Local Ad campaigns).
*   No existing manual promotions currently running on the campaign.

kept.heading: DO WE STILL NEED GOOGLE DISAVOW? (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google's Disavow tool is now mainly a recovery tool for sites hit with a manual action for unnatural links. kept.article_text:
Title: Do We Still Need Google Disavow?

URL Source: https://www.practicalecommerce.com/do-we-still-need-google-disavow

Published Time: 2026-09-07T13:17:29+00:00

Markdown Content:
Google launched the Disavow tool [in 2012](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2012/10/a-new-tool-to-disavow-links) to help websites neutralize the ranking harm of spammy backlinks.

Google has consistently warned website personnel that Disavow is an advanced feature to be used carefully. But link-related penalties are now rare, prompting some search optimizers to question the tool’s value.

I’ll address that dilemma in this article.

### Disavow can be useful

Google’s John Mueller [commented](https://www.reddit.com/r/SEO/comments/1w4mdsd/comment/p7bmxhn/) last week on Reddit that disavowing may still be worthwhile in certain cases. He also cautioned that disavowed links may take Google a few months to implement.

I advise today’s clients to use the Disavow tool only if their site incurred a link-related manual penalty as confirmed in “Security & Manual Actions” in Search Console and notified via the related email address.

Google’s Search Console Help article is broader, [suggesting](https://support.google.com/webmasters/answer/2648487?hl=en) the Disavow tool’s use for actual or _potential_ manual actions.

_If you have a manual action against your site for unnatural links to your site, or if you think you’re about to get such a manual action (because of paid links or other link schemes that violate our spam policies), you should try to remove the links from the other site to your site. If you can’t remove those links yourself, or get them removed, then you should disavow the URLs of the questionable pages or domains that link to your website._

Assessing the potential for a manual penalty seems daunting and likely unnecessary, given how rare it is. I look only for actual penalties.

### Manual vs. algorithmic

Memories of Google’s sitewide link-building penalties confuse the modern purpose of the Disavow tool.

In 2012, Google began penalizing websites algorithmically ([via the “Penguin” update](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2012/04/another-step-to-reward-high-quality)) for spammy link-building patterns. The Disavow tool was effective for recovering from those penalties despite the absence of manual actions.

In 2016, Google [announced](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2016/09/penguin-is-now-part-of-our-core) that Penguin was part of the [core algorithm](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/Google-Penguin-Now-Part-of-Core-Search-Algorithm), stating in part:

_Penguin is now more granular. Penguin now devalues spam by adjusting ranking based on spam signals, rather than affecting ranking of the whole site._

In other words, spammy backlinks no longer impact an entire site. Plus, such backlinks only trigger devalued authority signals to the linked page, not penalties.

Hence low-quality links can only impact page-specific rankings. Unless a site incurs a manual penalty as described above, there’s nothing to recover from or disavow.

Recovery in 2026 is not about fixing past tactics. What [does help](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/is-your-site-vulnerable-to-a-google-update) is quality content written for humans, a superior user experience, and outreach to trustworthy sites for meaningful links.

![Image 1: Ann Smarty](https://www.practicalecommerce.com/wp-content/uploads/userphoto/2425.jpg)

kept.heading: HOW NETFLIX MEASURES THE MARKETING YOU CANNOT A/B TEST (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Netflix uses geographic holdouts to measure channels that can't be A/B tested at the user level, including TV, OOH, and sponsorships. The approach measures incremental impact but requires careful decisions around test size, timing, media spillover, and carryover. Repeating tests builds stronger evidence, while campaigns without historical data require different methodologies. The challenge is getting leadership to protect test windows and accept the tradeoff between media delivery and measurement certainty.
kept.article_text:
Title: How Netflix Measures the Marketing You Cannot A/B Test

URL Source: https://karandhir.substack.com/p/how-netflix-measures-the-marketing

Published Time: 2026-09-02T18:01:30+00:00

Markdown Content:
The A/B testing era trained a generation of leaders to overlook something structural. Most of the money in a large portfolio can’t be randomized at the individual level. You can’t decide which person sees a billboard. You can’t withhold television from half the households in a market the way you withhold a checkout flow from half the visitors to a website. Sponsorships, audio, out-of-home, linear and much of streaming TV, a big share of upper-funnel video... all of it shares this property. Together, at most established brands, these channels carry the majority of spend.

For roughly 20 years the industry concluded these channels were unmeasurable in any causal sense, and it responded by taking platform and panel reporting on faith, or by defending the spend with narrative. The sophisticated measurement organizations concluded something else entirely. If you can’t randomize people, randomize markets. That conclusion, and the operating discipline built on top of it, is what this piece is about.

_The Design and Its Lineage_

A geo experiment randomizes geographic units instead of individuals. Some markets get the treatment. Some get held out. The causal effect is the difference in outcomes between the groups, adjusted for how the markets tracked each other before the intervention. Google published the foundational methodology in 2011, extended it with a time-based regression framework in 2017, and the design has since become the backbone of serious incrementality programs, because it works exactly where user-level randomization doesn’t.

The most consequential public demonstration is still the eBay study I’ve written about before. eBay shut off branded paid search in roughly 30% of U.S. designated market areas for 60 days and found the channel was producing near-zero incremental sales. Econometrica published the result after peer review at the highest level economics offers. For this series, the finding matters less than the instrument. The only reason eBay could learn what its attributed reporting would never tell it is that someone was willing to hold markets out.

Netflix industrialized the same design. Their engineering and data science teams have published enough public material about measuring marketing that can’t be A/B tested to assemble a clear picture, and the picture rewards close reading. Netflix randomizes at the television media-market level, because that’s the smallest unit at which TV can actually be bought in most countries. The team is candid that the binding constraint is small sample size. A country holds a limited number of media markets. The markets differ from each other. Statistical properties that hold comfortably at web scale fall apart at 20 or 50 geographic units. So they built tooling for exactly this regime, an internal package called Quasimodo, with a multivariate structure comparable to Google’s CausalImpact but extended to read more than a single intervention in a single region at a time.

Two details from Netflix’s public material deserve more attention than they get. First, the takedown is an experiment too. When Netflix runs out-of-home marketing in a set of markets and the campaign drove signups, removing it should send those markets back toward baseline, and that return is a second, independent read on the same effect. Put the campaign up in fresh markets afterward and you have a third. One expensive intervention becomes several measurements. That’s how a disciplined team buys statistical power it can’t get from sample size. Second, they’re honest about the no-pre-period problem. When Netflix promotes a show before launch, the success metric doesn’t exist yet... nobody can watch a show that hasn’t launched. Time-series counterfactual methods fail without history, and rather than forcing them, the team switches to member-level controls for those cases. Being willing to say this design doesn’t work here is a maturity marker most organizations haven’t reached.

_The Executive Decisions Inside a Geo Program_

The statistical machinery of geo experimentation is well documented and mostly commoditized at this point. What isn’t commoditized is the set of choices that determine whether a geo program produces answers anyone acts on. Every one of them is an executive decision wearing statistical clothing.

Start with power. Advertising effects are small relative to the natural variance of sales, a fact the economics literature established rigorously, and small effects require either large holdouts or long durations to detect. So there’s a direct trade between measurement quality and media delivery. A holdout big enough to produce a confident answer is a holdout big enough that the media team feels it and the sales organization notices which markets went dark. How much delivery to sacrifice for how much certainty isn’t a statistician’s call. It’s a leadership judgment about the value of knowing. Organizations that push it downward get holdouts sized for political comfort, which produce ambiguous results that everyone then reads according to their prior position.

Then contamination. Markets aren’t sealed containers. Media spills across borders, people commute, national buys resist clean localization, and a national promotion running through your test window washes over both cells. The leaders treat the experiment calendar as a governance object. National activity gets scheduled around high-priority tests, or the tests move, and someone with real authority owns that calendar. An organization that can’t protect a test window can’t run a geo program, whatever its statistical sophistication.

Persistence is the subtler trap. A market held out of television for 6 weeks measures the 6-week effect. It doesn’t tell you what a year of absence would do to the brand, and it misses carryover that lands after the window closes. Deciding what duration counts as an honest answer, and admitting the answer is bounded by the window, is again a leadership judgment. There’s no formula that removes the tension, and every honest geo program lives with it openly and prices it into the plan. The alternative is extrapolating a short-window read into a permanent budget conclusion, which is how organizations talk themselves into cutting channels whose effects they measured too briefly to see.

And repetition. A single geo test is an anecdote with confidence intervals. The Netflix pattern of on, off, and on again in fresh markets, plus the broader habit of retesting major channels on a rolling cadence, is what turns individual reads into stable understanding. This connects straight back to what I wrote in August about the experimentation muscle. The value compounds only when tests recur, feed model calibration, and accumulate in an archive the organization can query.

_What This Means for Your Organization_

I run measurement for a $1B portfolio, and the geo program is the part of the system I’d defend last if forced to cut. The models estimate every channel every quarter. The geo experiments are the only instrument that tells us, for the channels where the most money and the least user-level data live, whether those estimates deserve belief.

Here’s the standard I’d put in front of any leadership team. Every channel receiving 8 figures of annual investment should have a market-level causal read less than 24 months old, produced with a pre-registered analysis, adequate power, and a protected window. Channels that can’t meet the standard should carry an explicit uncertainty label in every planning conversation, so the organization knows which numbers are validated and which are assumed. Most organizations fail this standard. Not because the methodology is unavailable... because nobody with authority has demanded it, and downstream, the absence of demand reads as the absence of need.

The geo experiment is 2 decades old in its modern form. Published. Replicated. Industrialized by the best measurement teams in the world. The gap between organizations that run it as infrastructure and organizations that never run it isn’t a knowledge gap, it’s a commitment gap, and it shows up every planning cycle when 9 figures get reallocated on estimates nobody tested against a holdout.

Title: The AI hours nobody on your marketing team is counting

URL Source: https://www.growth-memo.com/p/the-ai-hours-nobody-on-your-marketing

Published Time: 2026-09-07T08:28:41+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XYTE!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fef6d2de7-8537-4d04-a00a-6ae358d2af43_1670x941.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XYTE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fef6d2de7-8537-4d04-a00a-6ae358d2af43_1670x941.png)

This Memo was sent to 29,114 subscribers. Welcome to +75 new readers! Sign up for free to get new insights every week, or sign up for Premium to get exclusive tools and frameworks that make you more effective.

Your marketing team has never spent more hours working in, on, and with AI. I think every marketer, especially every SEO, has this backlog of tools or shortcuts that they always wanted to build, unrestricted by engineering. But in the process, we end up building things that we could often pay (little money) for.

I’m pro AI use (that’s pretty clear if you’ve been reading for some time), and I’ve seen the positive impact of vibe coding and AI automation. But efficiency isn’t automatic. It comes from asking “when”, “what” and “why”.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m8xT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F975f5047-6947-4433-a0a0-8f1ad99af91f_2048x1982.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m8xT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F975f5047-6947-4433-a0a0-8f1ad99af91f_2048x1982.png)

In late 2025, [METR ran 16 experienced developers through 246 real tasks](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/), half with AI tools and half without.

The developers expected AI to make them 24% faster. It made them 19% slower. Even after seeing their completion times, they still believed AI had made them about 20% faster.

That gap is the AI productivity paradox. AI can make work feel faster while moving effort into prompting, waiting, checking, correcting, and maintaining the system. (The METR study above has since rerun the study in 2026 with [higher productivity but admittedly skewed results](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/#wider-adoption-of-ai-has-made-it-more-difficult-to-measure-task-level-productivity).)

Marketing teams are especially exposed because they’re building their own workflows. Every hour spent maintaining an internal tool is an hour not spent publishing, earning mentions, or strengthening the brand that search engines and AI systems recommend.

This new “homebrew AI work” doesn’t have the visibility of “real work,” so it’s often unaccounted for and the true cost is unanticipated. It’s “meta” work: working on how to get work done.

That cost is paid from somewhere, and organic visibility work often pays the bill.

[HubSpot reports 91% of marketing leaders](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/state-of-ai-report) say their teams use AI, and 66% say their company builds its own internal AI tools for marketing. Many of those projects don’t appear in your team’s marketing plan or project management tool.

Simply asking your marketing team whether internal AI tools are saving them time won’t actually tell you whether or not it’s doing so. Just like the 2025 METR study, they will say yes, they will mean it, **and they’ll probably be wrong.**

Growth marketers and organic search strategists are among the earliest adopters of AI tooling and workflows, because (1) understanding the technology is now a part of earning visibility inside it and (2) because LLMs are literally built on language, which is central to organic search and marketing overall.

The time it takes to learn, pressure test, and examine the technology is a requirement of the job now. It is also _real_ new work stacked on top of the old work, and the old work didn’t shrink.

This past year I have watched internal teams build custom AI workflows and tools, on top of the ones they already pay vendors for.

**Building your own in-house AI tools is addition, not necessarily efficiency.** While it feels like instant productivity, with a rush of extra dopamine on the side, it also involves maintenance over time.

AI doesn’t delete work, but instead removes work from _doing the task_ to building, learning, and maintaining the thing that does the task. That time investment shows up on no dashboard, and the bill for those hours? Often paid for by the work that has a longer lead time before it hits a strong ROI (like earning more organic AI mentions).

Your team isn’t an outlier when it comes to these hurdles, and the frustration surfaces when stakeholders ask why the AI tooling hasn’t paid off yet in scaled content production.

The AI work itself is a new production line item.

When 4 people working on the same marketing team each believe something different is happening, the fix is intentional communication. The AI SEO Change Management Plan is a 45-day implementation checklist plus a team education deck. [Premium subscribers get both](https://library.growth-memo.com/premium).

Your growth and organic search team’s new work is paid for out of the old work. The hours often come out of [content production, digital PR, community and UGC presence, and third-party review campaigns](https://www.growth-memo.com/p/multiply-your-brand-authority).

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XMaK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc02b58c4-dec4-420b-bad3-24b9036e2415_1638x2048.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XMaK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc02b58c4-dec4-420b-bad3-24b9036e2415_1638x2048.png)

BetterUp Labs and Stanford surveyed 1,150 full-time US workers about what they call [workslop: AI output that looks “finished”](https://hbr.org/2025/09/ai-generated-workslop-is-destroying-productivity) and isn’t.

*   41% got workslop in the previous month. Each time, it took an average of 1 hour and 56 minutes to sort out. At a 10,000-person company that runs past $9M a year.

*   The sender saved 20 minutes. Someone else spent 2 hours sifting through what was sent. On a dashboard that counts output, the sender looks great, like they saved time. The time savings were eaten elsewhere.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YLS1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdc49c2e8-f953-4960-94d1-e5bed0429129_2048x1858.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YLS1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdc49c2e8-f953-4960-94d1-e5bed0429129_2048x1858.png)

[Workday’s study puts a number on the rework](https://itbrief.news/story/ai-productivity-paradox-as-rework-erodes-time-gains): for every 10 hours AI saves, companies hand back about 4 in fixing and rewriting weak output. An [Upwork survey of 2,500 leaders and workers](https://www.upwork.com/research/ai-enhanced-work-models) reported the itemized version: Among employees who use AI and say it added to their workload, 39% point to time spent checking and fixing AI output, 23% to learning the tools, and 21% to just being handed more work.

Before your team builds it, check whether the answer is already in the premium library. 45+ checklists, light tools, AI workflows, and stakeholder decks.

When marketing attention gets pulled, the work with a slower ROI or murkier attribution is what gives to the meta work of homebrew AI or wading through workslop. The unsexy, unglamorous work that multiplies brand authority is often the production flexible enough to steal time from, because it’s a longer-term play for customers. Things like:

*   Publishing enough depth on a topic that you become the obvious source

*   Earning mentions on the sites AI answers actually pull from

*   Showing up in the Reddit and YouTube threads your buyers read

None of that work produces a quickly visible result or an easily attributable lead, sometimes for weeks or months after the work is initiated. (Even though some of the tasks can be automated with AI.)

If you want to see what that compounding work looks like in practice, this Memo’s sponsor Semrush shows which brands are winning and the strategies behind their visibility latest in the AI Visibility Index.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cmGF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff72a5e4e-d557-4462-9075-36bb0bbb0caf_900x450.png)](https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=influencers&utm_campaign=socialorganic_partners_growthmemo&utm_term=social_organic&utm_content=kevinindig_september07)

Semrush has published its biggest AI visibility study yet, covering seven months of data alongside free playbooks and studies that unpack the trends and tactics behind the winners.

The analysis draws from:

*   126M+ real AI search prompts

*   22 industries

*   4 AI platforms

*   Thousands of brands

See who made the leaderboards, why they’re on top, and what you can borrow from their strategy.

[Explore the AI Visibility Index](https://ai-visibility-index.semrush.com/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=influencers&utm_campaign=socialorganic_partners_growthmemo&utm_term=social_organic&utm_content=kevinindig_september07)

That opportunity cost may be one reason teams resist adopting custom AI workflows.

A workflow works on the day you finish it. All the time spent in meetings, AI engineering, and team (ie, _user_) interviews exists as work even _prior to_ having the usable workflow.

Then, on the first day it’s used by your team, it immediately starts to degrade.

Then the model version changes, or someone surfaces an issue or hurdle that appeared when using it. The tool it plugs into ships an update, and the thing stops working on a Tuesday, and it throws a wrench in the rest of the week. (In Part 2, we’ll discuss how to avoid some of this.)

From a practical perspective, every single workflow your team builds creates a small permanent job to maintain. Those jobs accumulate over time.

**What your executives think is happening:** You’re using AI to build more efficient workflows and save time and money.

**What your individual contributors think is happening:** AI doesn’t work right. Every output they receive needs deep revision or a workflow or project doc needs regular updating and tweaking to solve.

**What your strategists think is happening:** Tons of time spent on workflows, not enough resources to invest in growing and repairing brand visibility in organic search.

**What is**_**really**_**happening:** The team is building tools to make the brand work faster, and the brand work is often moved to the back burner. The tools and workflows will get finished (or tossed/replaced) eventually. The 9 months of citations, mentions, and reviews that were not earned this year cannot be backdated.

The job must have an owner, and the owner often is whoever built it (which isn’t always the right person long-term). The owner is the only one who knows what it does when it breaks, so when they take PTO, the task reverts to manual until they’re back.

None of that maintenance shows up anywhere over time on your marketing team (unless you hire a position for this responsibility alone, like a content engineer or marketing engineer), same as the build.

**This isn’t an argument against building.** I am building and testing new things for myself and my clients continuously, and building is essential.

But this has shown me that homebrew AI is still uneven. It genuinely collapses some tasks and quietly makes others much slower, and the 2 look identical from the distance of your leadership board (until somebody has spent 3 weeks on building and fixing something).

For smart marketing leaders, the skill worth developing right now is being able to clearly name and defend:

1/ When an AI workflow or automation makes sense for your team, and when it doesn’t and

2/ When AI work experimentation is increasing efficiency vs draining time from the real brand-building, lead-generating work.

Don’t reinvent the wheel. I (Kevin) made this mistake at Shopify when I was leading a small army of engineers: I spent way too much of their capacity building tools from scratch that we could buy, which prevented us from building more impactful work. Skip doing this to your growth team.

If you’re trying to work out which AI projects are worth the hours, this month we’re releasing tools and frameworks to help you guide these conversations and decisions with stakeholders in the premium resource library. Keep an eye out.

Next in Part 2: which of this work to buy, which to hand to someone who has already built it, and how to build and manage the right kind of AI work that is left.

kept.article_text:
Title: Why Nvidia is buying Hugging Face

URL Source: https://cafetechinenglish.substack.com/p/why-nvidia-is-buying-hugging-face

Published Time: 2026-09-07T12:31:39+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YvpE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F35b3a668-2fdd-4c92-bb99-e45a8ddce088_1067x533.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YvpE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F35b3a668-2fdd-4c92-bb99-e45a8ddce088_1067x533.webp)

Over the past few months, Jensen Huang had repeatedly emphasized the importance of open models in the development of generative artificial intelligence. On Thursday, Nvidia’s CEO turned words into action, announcing the acquisition of Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. Founded by three French entrepreneurs in New York and based in Paris for a time, the startup has become the leading hub for open-source AI: its library now hosts three million models and 500,000 datasets and is used by 18 million developers.

The deal still requires approval from competition authorities. That outcome is far from guaranteed, given that Nvidia is already facing several antitrust investigations on both sides of the Atlantic over its dominant position in the market for chips designed for generative AI. The Santa Clara-based company nevertheless remains confident and hopes to complete the acquisition in the first half of 2027. If completed, it would be the largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history — excluding the $20 billion disguised acquisition of chipmaker Groq carried out earlier this year.

Launched in 2016, Hugging Face initially set out to build a chatbot aimed at teenagers — a _“Tamagotchi powered by artificial intelligence”_ designed to entertain them and become their friend. Despite enjoying some early success, the project was short-lived. The startup then pivoted toward a large library initially focused on machine learning — algorithms capable of learning on their own — and gradually expanded into large language models. The launch of ChatGPT and the rapid rise of generative AI subsequently propelled the company into an entirely new dimension.

Hugging Face now plays a central role in open-source AI, giving developers access to models for text and image generation, transcription, and visual recognition. Over the years, the platform has expanded considerably. It now offers paid services with a wide range of tools for testing, adapting, and deploying models. The company claims to have more than 200,000 corporate customers. According to _The Information_, Hugging Face crossed the $150 million annualized revenue mark in August, up 50% in just two months.

Nvidia is not acquiring the company for its commercial potential, however. Even with significant acceleration, Hugging Face’s revenue would remain a drop in the ocean compared with Nvidia’s own sales, which are expected to surpass $1 billion for the first time in the third quarter. The Santa Clara-based giant is primarily seeking to maintain _“a healthy ecosystem bringing together both providers of proprietary models and open models,”_ explains Justin Boitano, vice president of Enterprise AI. _“We will benefit from this through the training and inference workloads running on our chips,”_ he adds.

_“We will be able to scale up and maximize our impact on the industry,”_ says Clément Delangue, Hugging Face’s founder and CEO. He has set an ambitious goal: reaching 100 million developers. By fostering the development of open-source AI, Nvidia can hope to accelerate the democratization of artificial intelligence, particularly among businesses. Lower costs should translate into stronger demand for its graphics processors. The company also wants to support a broad ecosystem of model developers beyond the industry giants, which are increasingly relying on chips designed in-house.

The acquisition of Hugging Face fits into a strategy Nvidia has already been pursuing: using part of its enormous profits to support as many players as possible across the generative-AI ecosystem. The company has invested tens of billions of dollars in OpenAI and Anthropic. It is also one of the most active investors in so-called neoclouds, new companies specializing in AI-focused computing power. The goal is to ensure that these major customers have the funding they need to grow — and, in turn, continue buying Nvidia’s graphics processors at scale.

One question remains: how will regulators respond to the acquisition of the leading distribution platform for open-source models by the near-hegemonic player in AI chips? In 2022, Nvidia had to abandon its planned acquisition of Arm Holdings, which occupies a position partly comparable to Hugging Face’s role in processor architectures.

Nvidia has pledged to keep the service _“neutral and open”_ and insists that the deal will help prevent AI from becoming concentrated in the hands of a handful of tech giants. The company may nevertheless have to make commitments to limit software integration and ensure that its competitors are not disadvantaged.

Title: Attention Is Rented. Memory Is the New Media. | LBBOnline

URL Source: https://lbbonline.com/news/Attention-Is-Rented-Memory-Is-the-New-Media

Published Time: 2026-09-07T08:13:10.801Z

Markdown Content:
“If no one tells a story about it tomorrow, it didn't happen.”

Is a line we live by at BLACKLIST, and it's at the heart of our first trend report.

We started this agency to work in the space where brands actually meet people, in real life. A decade later, that space is where the industry's most interesting brands are spending their money. 'THE REAL ALGORITHM IS MEMORY' is our read on why, built from a survey of hundreds of senior industry voices across agency leadership, brand strategy and experiential, and layered against industry research.

The core idea is simple. Reach and impressions tell you who saw something. They say nothing about who kept it. Nearly half the people we surveyed, 47%, said the real value of experiential lives in long-term brand memory rather than in-the-moment impact. When we asked what actually cuts through in a saturated media environment, emotional intensity came first. Physical presence in a digital world came second.

![Image 1](https://d3q27bh1u24u2o.cloudfront.net/wysiwyg/news/2026-09/Image-4.sqR4M_sd.png)

We work almost exclusively in entertainment for clients including Disney, Pokémon, SkyShowtime, Lionsgate and Paramount. Fans don't just want to watch these worlds anymore, they want to walk into them. Nearly half buy IP-related products specifically to extend the connection beyond the screen. A quarter say community, not ownership, is what pulls them in. Netflix House is the clearest signal of where this goes: not an activation with an end date, but a permanent address.

The report maps seven shifts we're seeing play out across OOH, pop-ups and physical brand experience right now, from billboards behaving like public art to buildings becoming media in their own right. The one that anchors the whole thesis is about what actually lasts. Most stunts are built to generate a moment of coverage, then fade.The work we think is winning is built to generate a story that stays with people and gets repeated. When Apple dropped a replica Lumon Industries office into Grand Central Terminal for Severance, full cast in character, thousands of commuters stopped without anyone asking them to. People were still talking about it days later.One approach gets you a press release. The other gets you a memory.

![Image 2](https://d3q27bh1u24u2o.cloudfront.net/wysiwyg/news/2026-09/Image-5.dlqBmH9q.png)

None of this is a rejection of digital. The internet still amplifies culture. But somewhere along the way, everything in every feed started looking, feeling and disappearing the same way, and everyone started calling it slop. Real life is where culture is sticking right now, and the brands who've figured that out are already quietly winning, even if their dashboards haven't caught up to yet.

That's the gap this report is written for. Attention is rented. Memory is owned. That's the algorithm now, and we'd argue nobody in the entertainment and gaming space is building for it more deliberately than we are.

‘THE REAL ALGORITHM IS MEMORY’ is available now [here](http://blacklistcreative.com/).
